/*
 * CSE 470 - Software Engineering
 * Refactoring Practice Problem - SOLUTION (Java)
 *
 * Semester Fee Processing System, refactored.
 *
 * External behaviour is unchanged: this file prints exactly what the
 * original smelly version printed. Every comment below names the smell
 * that was present in the original code and the Fowler refactoring used
 * to remove it.
 */

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
// FIXES: Duplicated Code (data level)
//   Original: RATE = 4500.0 and LATE = 0.05 were declared TWICE - once in
//   FeeMgr and once in FeeReport. Two copies of the same constant drift
//   apart the moment one of them is updated.
//   Refactoring: Pull Up Field - one authoritative home for the rates.
//
// FIXES: Inappropriate Naming
//   Original: RATE and LATE said nothing about what they measure.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
final class FeeRates {
    public static final double PER_CREDIT = 4500.0;
    public static final double LATE_SURCHARGE = 0.05;
    public static final double LOW_ATTENDANCE_PENALTY = 1000.0;
    public static final double WAIVER_DISCOUNT_MULTIPLIER = 0.8;
    public static final double HIGH_DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.1;
    public static final double STANDARD_DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.05;
    public static final int HIGH_DISCOUNT_CREDIT_THRESHOLD = 9;

    private FeeRates() {
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
// FIXES: Inappropriate Naming
//   Original: class AttRange with fields l and h.
//   Refactoring: Rename Class / Rename Variable.
//
// FIXES: Feature Envy
//   Original: AttPolicy pulled getLow() and getHigh() out of AttRange and
//   did the comparison itself. Data and the behaviour that acts on it
//   belong together, so the comparison now lives here.
//   Refactoring: Move Method.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
class AttendanceRange {
    private final int low;
    private final int high;

    public AttendanceRange(int low, int high) {
        // FIXES: Comments (Introduce Assertion)
        //   Original: preconditions on the data were never stated at all -
        //   a nonsensical range would have silently produced a wrong fee.
        assert low <= high : "attendance low must not exceed high";
        this.low = low;
        this.high = high;
    }

    public int getLow() {
        return low;
    }

    public int getHigh() {
        return high;
    }

    public boolean isWithin(int minimumLow, int maximumHigh) {
        return low >= minimumLow && high <= maximumHigh;
    }
}

class AttendancePolicy {
    public static final int MINIMUM_ATTENDANCE = 60;
    public static final int MAXIMUM_ATTENDANCE = 100;

    // FIXES: Long Parameter List / Long Method (Preserve Whole Object)
    //   Original: withinRange(low, high) forced every caller to write
    //       int low  = s.getAtt().getLow();
    //       int high = s.getAtt().getHigh();
    //       boolean ok = policy.withinRange(low, high);
    //   Refactoring: pass the whole object; the two unpacking lines vanish.
    public boolean isAcceptable(AttendanceRange attendance) {
        return attendance.isWithin(MINIMUM_ATTENDANCE, MAXIMUM_ATTENDANCE);
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
// FIXES: Long Parameter List (Introduce Parameter Object)
//   Original: calc() took sd, sm, sy, ed, em, ey - six loose integers that
//   always travelled together and always meant the same two dates.
//   Refactoring: Introduce Parameter Object - SimpleDate and Term.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
class SimpleDate {
    private final int day;
    private final int month;
    private final int year;

    public SimpleDate(int day, int month, int year) {
        this.day = day;
        this.month = month;
        this.year = year;
    }

    public int getMonth() {
        return month;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return day + "/" + month + "/" + year;
    }
}

class Term {
    private final String label;
    private final SimpleDate start;
    private final SimpleDate end;

    public Term(String label, SimpleDate start, SimpleDate end) {
        this.label = label;
        this.start = start;
        this.end = end;
    }

    // FIXES: Long Method (Extract Method)
    //   Original: the condition read `!(em - sm > 4)`, a raw arithmetic
    //   expression buried inside an already unreadable if-statement.
    public boolean spansMoreThan(int months) {
        return end.getMonth() - start.getMonth() > months;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return label + " " + start + " - " + end;
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
// FIXES: Refused Bequest (Push Down Method)
//   Original: Member declared getScholarshipPercent(), getTranscript() and
//   payTuition(). VisitingStudent inherited all three and then refused the
//   bequest - returning 0, returning "", and leaving payTuition empty.
//   Refactoring: Push Down Method. Member now holds identity only, so
//   there is nothing left for a subclass to neuter.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
class Member {
    private final String memberId;
    private final String name;

    public Member(String memberId, String name) {
        this.memberId = memberId;
        this.name = name;
    }

    public String getId() {
        return memberId;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }
}

class RegularStudent extends Member {
    // FIXES: Inappropriate Naming
    //   Original: fields cr, p, w, a, f and accessor getAtt().
    //   Refactoring: Rename Variable / Rename Method.
    private final int credits;
    private final String program;
    private final String waiver;
    private final AttendanceRange attendance;
    private final List<Double> courseFees;

    public RegularStudent(String memberId, String name, int credits,
                          String program, String waiver,
                          AttendanceRange attendance, List<Double> courseFees) {
        super(memberId, name);
        this.credits = credits;
        this.program = program;
        this.waiver = waiver;
        this.attendance = attendance;
        this.courseFees = courseFees;
    }

    public int getCredits() {
        return credits;
    }

    public String getProgram() {
        return program;
    }

    public String getWaiver() {
        return waiver;
    }

    public AttendanceRange getAttendance() {
        return attendance;
    }

    public List<Double> getCourseFees() {
        return courseFees;
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------
    // FIXES: Feature Envy (Move Method)
    //   Original: RegularStudent was a bag of getters. FeeMgr and FeeReport
    //   reached into it over and over - getCredits(), getProgram(),
    //   getWaiver(), getFees(), getAtt() - and did all the arithmetic
    //   themselves. The behaviour below is now where its data lives.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------

    // FIXES: Duplicated Code (literal AND semantic levels)
    //   Original literal duplication: the loop
    //       for (double x : s.getFees()) { tmp = tmp + x; }
    //   was copied verbatim into FeeMgr.proc and FeeReport.build.
    //   Original semantic duplication: FeeMgr.calc summed the very same
    //   list with an index-driven while loop - same intent, different
    //   shape, so it did not even look like a duplicate.
    //   Refactoring: Extract Method + Substitute Algorithm. One summation.
    public double totalCourseFees() {
        double total = 0.0;
        for (double fee : courseFees) {
            total = total + fee;
        }
        return total;
    }

    // FIXES: Long Method (Replace Temp with Query)
    //   Original: `double base = s.getCredits() * FeeMgr.RATE;` was a temp
    //   that the rest of calc() leaned on. If the base-fee formula changes,
    //   it must now change in exactly one place.
    public double baseFee() {
        return credits * FeeRates.PER_CREDIT;
    }

    // FIXES: Long Method (Decompose Conditional) / conditional complexity
    //   Original: a seven-clause boolean mixing &&, || and two negations
    //   sat inline in calc(). Nobody could read it aloud, let alone test it.
    //       if (s.getProgram().equals("CSE") && s.getCredits() > 9
    //               && !s.getWaiver().equals("NONE")
    //               && !(em - sm > 4)
    //               && (s.getCredits() < 15 || s.getWaiver().equals("MERIT"))
    //               && s.getAtt().getLow() >= 60
    //               && !isLate) {
    //   Refactoring: Decompose Conditional - extract the condition into a
    //   named predicate, then extract its parts into named predicates too.
    public boolean qualifiesForWaiverDiscount(Term term, boolean isLate) {
        return isInDiscountedProgram()
                && carriesEnoughCredits()
                && holdsAWaiver()
                && !term.spansMoreThan(4)
                && waiverStillApplies()
                && meetsMinimumAttendance()
                && !isLate;
    }

    private boolean isInDiscountedProgram() {
        return program.equals("CSE");
    }

    private boolean carriesEnoughCredits() {
        return credits > 9;
    }

    private boolean holdsAWaiver() {
        return !waiver.equals("NONE");
    }

    private boolean waiverStillApplies() {
        return credits < 15 || waiver.equals("MERIT");
    }

    private boolean meetsMinimumAttendance() {
        return attendance.getLow() >= AttendancePolicy.MINIMUM_ATTENDANCE;
    }

    // FIXES: Long Parameter List (Replace Parameter with Method)
    //   Original: calc() accepted discountLevel as its eleventh parameter,
    //   and main() computed it from the student it was already passing in:
    //       int d = 1;
    //       if (st.getCredits() > 9) { d = 2; }
    //   The callee can ask the student itself, so the parameter is dropped.
    public double discountRate() {
        if (credits > FeeRates.HIGH_DISCOUNT_CREDIT_THRESHOLD) {
            return FeeRates.HIGH_DISCOUNT_RATE;
        }
        return FeeRates.STANDARD_DISCOUNT_RATE;
    }

    // FIXES: Duplicated Code (logical-steps level)
    //   Original: the identical three-step check - empty id, non-positive
    //   credits, empty program - was written out in FeeMgr.calc,
    //   FeeMgr.proc and FeeReport.build. Three copies of one rule.
    // FIXES: Comments
    //   Original: each copy was introduced by the comment
    //       // step 1: make sure the record is usable
    //   A comment labelling a block is a request to extract that block into
    //   a method whose name says what the comment said.
    //   Refactoring: Extract Method + Move Method (the rule is about the
    //   student's own data, so it belongs on the student).
    public boolean hasValidRecord() {
        if (getId().equals("")) {
            System.out.println("bad id");
            return false;
        }
        if (credits <= 0) {
            System.out.println("bad credits");
            return false;
        }
        if (program.equals("")) {
            System.out.println("bad program");
            return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    public int getScholarshipPercent() {
        return 25;
    }

    public String getTranscript() {
        return "TRANSCRIPT OF " + getName();
    }

    public void payTuition(double amount) {
        System.out.println(getName() + " paid " + amount);
    }
}

class VisitingStudent extends Member {
    // FIXES: Refused Bequest (Push Down Method)
    //   Original: this class existed almost entirely to cancel what it
    //   inherited - three overrides that returned 0, returned "" and did
    //   nothing, each apologised for by a comment. Now that Member carries
    //   no degree-student behaviour, VisitingStudent refuses nothing and
    //   needs no overrides at all.
    public VisitingStudent(String memberId, String name) {
        super(memberId, name);
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
// FIXES: Refused Bequest (Push Down Method)
//   Original: VisitingStudent carried three do-nothing overrides because
//   Member forced degree-student behaviour on every subclass. The rules
//   for a non-degree member are stated once, here, outside the hierarchy,
//   so no class has to fake an implementation it does not want.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
class NonDegreeMemberPolicy {
    public int scholarshipPercent(Member member) {
        return 0;
    }

    public String transcript(Member member) {
        return "";
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
// FIXES: Duplicated Code (conceptual level)
//   Original: FeeMgr.sortFees was a bubble sort and FeeReport.sortFees was
//   a selection sort. Two different algorithms solving one problem is
//   duplication even though not a single line matches.
//   Refactoring: Substitute Algorithm - keep one implementation.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
final class FeeSorting {
    public static double[] sortedFees(double[] fees) {
        double[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(fees, fees.length);
        Arrays.sort(copy);
        return copy;
    }

    private FeeSorting() {
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
// FIXES: Inappropriate Naming
//   Original: class FeeMgr, methods calc() and proc(). "Mgr" is an
//   abbreviation, "calc" does not say what it calculates, and "proc" says
//   nothing whatsoever.
//   Refactoring: Rename Class / Rename Method.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------
class FeeCalculator {

    // FIXES: Long Method (Extract Method, Replace Temp with Query,
    //        Decompose Conditional, Preserve Whole Object)
    // FIXES: Long Parameter List (11 parameters -> 4)
    //   Original signature:
    //       double calc(RegularStudent s, int sd, int sm, int sy, int ed,
    //                   int em, int ey, String label, boolean isLate,
    //                   AttPolicy policy, int discountLevel)
    //   Original body: ~50 lines doing six unrelated jobs - validating,
    //   choosing a rate, summing fees, checking attendance, discounting,
    //   applying a late surcharge and printing a header.
    public double calculateSemesterFee(RegularStudent student, Term term,
                                       boolean isLate, AttendancePolicy policy) {
        if (!student.hasValidRecord()) {
            return 0.0;
        }

        double total = feeAfterWaiver(student, term, isLate);
        total += student.totalCourseFees();
        total += attendancePenalty(student, policy);
        total -= student.baseFee() * student.discountRate();
        total += lateSurcharge(total, isLate);

        System.out.println(term);
        return total;
    }

    private double feeAfterWaiver(RegularStudent student, Term term,
                                  boolean isLate) {
        if (student.qualifiesForWaiverDiscount(term, isLate)) {
            return student.baseFee() * FeeRates.WAIVER_DISCOUNT_MULTIPLIER;
        }
        return student.baseFee();
    }

    private double attendancePenalty(RegularStudent student,
                                     AttendancePolicy policy) {
        // FIXES: Long Method - the original wrote
        //       if (ok == false) { total = total + 1000.0; }
        //   with a magic number and a redundant `== false` comparison.
        if (policy.isAcceptable(student.getAttendance())) {
            return 0.0;
        }
        return FeeRates.LOW_ATTENDANCE_PENALTY;
    }

    private double lateSurcharge(double amount, boolean isLate) {
        if (isLate) {
            return amount * FeeRates.LATE_SURCHARGE;
        }
        return 0.0;
    }

    // FIXES: Duplicated Code (literal + semantic) and Feature Envy
    //   Original: proc() re-validated the record and re-summed the fee list
    //   with its own copy of the loop. Both jobs now belong to the student.
    public double totalCourseFees(RegularStudent student) {
        if (!student.hasValidRecord()) {
            return 0.0;
        }
        return student.totalCourseFees();
    }
}

class FeeReport {

    // FIXES: Duplicated Code (literal, data and logical-steps levels)
    //   Original: build() carried its own copy of the validation sequence,
    //   its own copy of the summing loop, and its own copy of the RATE
    //   constant. All three are now shared.
    // FIXES: Feature Envy
    //   Original: this method computed s.getCredits() * RATE + tmp, doing
    //   the student's arithmetic on the student's data.
    public String build(RegularStudent student) {
        if (!student.hasValidRecord()) {
            return "";
        }

        double total = student.baseFee() + student.totalCourseFees();
        return student.getName() + " | " + student.getProgram() + " | "
                + student.getCredits() + " cr | " + total;
    }
}

public class FeeSystemSolution {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AttendanceRange attendance = new AttendanceRange(75, 95);
        List<Double> courseFees = new ArrayList<Double>();
        courseFees.add(1200.0);
        courseFees.add(800.0);
        courseFees.add(950.0);
        RegularStudent student = new RegularStudent("24141001", "Rafi", 12,
                "CSE", "MERIT", attendance, courseFees);

        FeeCalculator calculator = new FeeCalculator();
        FeeReport report = new FeeReport();
        AttendancePolicy policy = new AttendancePolicy();

        // FIXES: Long Parameter List (Introduce Parameter Object)
        //   Original call site passed six loose date components plus a label.
        Term spring = new Term("Spring 2026", new SimpleDate(1, 1, 2026),
                new SimpleDate(15, 5, 2026));

        // FIXES: Long Parameter List (Replace Parameter with Method)
        //   Original: main computed the discount level here and passed it
        //   in. That block is gone - the student answers the question itself.
        System.out.println(
                calculator.calculateSemesterFee(student, spring, false, policy));
        System.out.println(calculator.totalCourseFees(student));
        System.out.println(report.build(student));

        // FIXES: Duplicated Code (conceptual level)
        //   Original: two calls to two different sorting algorithms.
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(
                FeeSorting.sortedFees(new double[]{950.0, 800.0, 1200.0})));
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(
                FeeSorting.sortedFees(new double[]{950.0, 800.0, 1200.0})));

        // FIXES: Refused Bequest (Push Down Method)
        //   Original:
        //       VisitingStudent v = new VisitingStudent("24141002", "Nadia");
        //       System.out.println(v.getScholarshipPercent()); // returns 0
        //       System.out.println(v.getTranscript());         // returns ""
        //       v.payTuition(5000.0);                          // does nothing
        //   Scholarships, transcripts and tuition now live on RegularStudent
        //   only. The empty payTuition call disappears entirely - a call that
        //   did nothing is not worth keeping - and the two "not applicable"
        //   answers come from an explicit policy object instead of being
        //   hidden inside do-nothing overrides.
        VisitingStudent visiting = new VisitingStudent("24141002", "Nadia");
        NonDegreeMemberPolicy nonDegree = new NonDegreeMemberPolicy();
        System.out.println(nonDegree.scholarshipPercent(visiting));
        System.out.println(nonDegree.transcript(visiting));
    }
}

Every FIXES: comment in the listing names the smell that was present and the refactoring used to remove it. Those comments are teaching scaffolding — in real code they would be deleted, because the point of the refactoring is that the code no longer needs them.

Every change, by smell

SmellWhat changedRefactorings
1 · Inappropriate namingEvery class, field, method and constant renamed to say what it is. FeeMgr → FeeCalculator, calc → calculateSemesterFee, proc → totalCourseFees, RATE → FeeRates.PER_CREDIT.Rename Variable / Method / Class / Field
2 · CommentsThe three “step 1” blocks became hasValidRecord(). The two why comments on visiting students survive. A precondition was added to AttendanceRange.Extract Method, Move Method, Introduce Assertion
3 · Long methodcalc — 39 code lines, six jobs — became calculateSemesterFee at 10 lines plus three named private helpers. The seven-clause conditional became six named predicates.Extract Method, Replace Temp with Query, Decompose Conditional
4 · Long parameter listEleven parameters became four. Six date components became Term/SimpleDate; discountLevel became student.discountRate(); the unpacked attendance bounds became policy.isAcceptable(attendance).Introduce Parameter Object, Replace Parameter with Method, Preserve Whole Object
5 · Feature envyThe fee arithmetic moved onto RegularStudent; the range comparison moved onto AttendanceRange. FeeReport formats and nothing else.Move Method
6 · Duplicated codeOne summation, one validation, one sort, one set of constants. All five levels addressed.Extract Method, Substitute Algorithm, Pull Up Field
7 · Refused bequestMember reduced to identity. The three degree-student methods pushed down to RegularStudent; the non-degree answers moved into an explicit NonDegreeMemberPolicy.Push Down Method, Extract Class

Verify it yourself

cd refactoring

python3 fee_system.py            > /tmp/a.txt
python3 fee_system_solution.py   > /tmp/b.txt
javac -d /tmp/p FeeSystem.java         && java -cp /tmp/p FeeSystem          > /tmp/c.txt
javac -d /tmp/s FeeSystemSolution.java && java -cp /tmp/s FeeSystemSolution  > /tmp/d.txt

md5sum /tmp/a.txt /tmp/b.txt /tmp/c.txt /tmp/d.txt   # four identical hashes

Three changes the output does not show

Sorting is no longer in place. The original sortFees mutated the caller's list and returned it; sorted_fees / FeeSorting.sortedFees returns a new list and leaves the argument alone. No caller here depends on the mutation, so nothing printed changes — but a caller elsewhere would notice.

A call disappeared. v.payTuition(5000.0) invoked an empty method body, so removing it removes nothing observable. Deleting a call is only safe when you have checked that the call does nothing, which is precisely what made it a refused bequest.

An assertion was added. AttendanceRange now rejects low > high. It passes for this data, and in Java it is not even evaluated unless you run with -ea.

Where the reference solution made a judgement call

NonDegreeMemberPolicy is one way to state the non-degree rules outside the hierarchy; its two methods currently ignore the member they receive. The alternative — a Billable interface that RegularStudent implements and VisitingStudent does not — pushes the same decision into the type system and is the better answer in a larger program. Either is worth full marks with the reasoning stated.

Similarly, FeeCalculator.totalCourseFees(student) survives as a one-line pass-through so that the second line of output still comes from the calculator. If you deleted it and called student.total_course_fees() from main instead, the output is identical and the design is arguably cleaner — say so and it counts.

Marking summary

  • Naming — no abbreviations, no single letters, method names name their result.
  • Comments — no comment describes what; both why comments survive.
  • Long method — nothing over about a dozen lines; the big conditional is decomposed into named predicates.
  • Parameters — four or fewer on the fee entry point; no parameter the callee could derive itself.
  • Feature envy — arithmetic lives with the data; FeeReport only formats.
  • Duplication — one summation, one validation, one sort, one copy of each constant.
  • Refused bequest — no empty bodies, no placeholder returns, Member holds identity only.
  • Behaviour — diff against the original output is empty. A submission that fails this fails the exercise, however clean the code is.
CSE470Software Engineering

Design Patterns — practice problems & solutions

Fifteen problems on Observer, Singleton, Adapter and Factory Method — eight that drill one pattern each, seven that make two patterns work together. Every solution comes with a UML class diagram, a reference implementation in both Python and Java, the real program output, the participant table, and the marking points.

The four patterns

Observer

Define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically.

Removes the coupling fault: the subject stops knowing who is listening.

Drilled in: The Section Notice Board, The Online Auction Room, Campus Alert Hub, Flood Warning Station

Singleton

Ensure a class has only one instance, and provide a global point of access to it.

Removes the scarcity / shared-state fault: one sequence, one connection, one cache.

Drilled in: One Grade Database, One Print Spooler for the Lab, Campus Alert Hub, The Card Reader, The Campus SMS Gateway, The Currency Desk, IT Helpdesk Tickets

Adapter

Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect.

Removes the vocabulary fault: the client stops speaking the vendor's language.

Drilled in: Checkout with Two Payment Vendors, Two Book Search Back-ends, Flood Warning Station, The Upload Service, The Card Reader, The Campus SMS Gateway, The Currency Desk

Factory Method

Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

Removes the selection fault: the shared routine stops deciding what to build.

Drilled in: The Courier Branch, The Result Export Portals, The Upload Service, IT Helpdesk Tickets

How to use this page

Read the story, write your own solution, then reveal the reference one. The Reveal solution button on each problem — and the Solutions switch in the top bar — control that.

Every code block has Python and Java tabs. The two implementations are the same design, not the same code: wherever the languages genuinely disagree — __new__ versus a private constructor, multiple inheritance versus one extends, tuples versus a small class — there is a Java notes panel in the solution explaining the difference. Those differences are worth as much class time as the patterns.

Because only one problem is on screen at a time, your browser's find-in-page cannot see the others. The filter box makes up for it: type three or more characters and it searches the full text of every problem, not just the titles — a vendor method name, a variable, or a phrase from any code sample will find the problem it belongs to.

Keyboard shortcuts: / to filter the list, [ and ] for the previous and next problem, l to flip the code language, s to toggle solutions. Printing gives you whatever is on screen — a clean problem sheet with solutions hidden, a solution key with them shown.

Reading the diagrams

Class boxes show the name, then the fields and methods that matter to the pattern — not the whole class. Italic names are abstract or interfaces; «singleton» marks a class that guards its own instance count.

Pattern skeletons

The shape every solution in this pack is an instance of — one runnable skeleton per pattern, and a map from all fifteen problems onto it.

Each skeleton below is a complete program. Copy it, run it, and watch what it prints. Then open any problem and read its solution as this skeleton with the roles renamed — the class names change, the shape does not.

That is the point of the tables at the end of each section: they say exactly which class in each problem plays which role. If a solution ever seems to put a method somewhere unexpected, check it against the rules list — the rules hold in every one of the fifteen.

Observer

Intent

Define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically.

Four classes, always in this order. Observer is the interface the subject calls back through. Subject is a concrete base class that owns the list and the three list operations — you write it once and never change it. ConcreteSubject extends it, holds the real state, and calls notify() at the end of every state-changing operation. The concrete observers implement update and read the state back out through the subject's getters.

RoleWhat it doesNotes
ObserverThe callback interface. One abstract method, update(subject).Nothing else ever goes here.
SubjectOwns _observers, attach, detach, notify. Identical in every problem.Note __init__ lives here, not in the child.
ConcreteSubjectExtends Subject. Holds the state, and calls self.notify() at the end of each state change.Must call super().__init__().
Concrete ObserversImplement update(subject) and read state through the subject's getters.They never read each other.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# ---------- Observer interface ----------
class Observer(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def update(self, subject):
        pass


# ---------- Subject ----------
class Subject:
    def __init__(self):
        self._observers = []

    def attach(self, observer):
        self._observers.append(observer)

    def detach(self, observer):
        if observer in self._observers:
            self._observers.remove(observer)

    def notify(self):
        for observer in self._observers:
            observer.update(self)


# ---------- Concrete Subject ----------
class ConcreteSubject(Subject):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()          # never forget this line
        self._state = None

    def change(self, value):        # the state-changing operation ...
        self._state = value
        self.notify()               # ... always ends with notify()

    def get_state(self):            # one reader per piece of state
        return self._state


# ---------- Concrete Observers ----------
class ConcreteObserverA(Observer):
    def update(self, subject):
        state = subject.get_state()          # pull, then print
        print(f"A saw {state}")


class ConcreteObserverB(Observer):
    def update(self, subject):
        state = subject.get_state()
        print(f"B saw {state}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    subject = ConcreteSubject()
    a = ConcreteObserverA()
    b = ConcreteObserverB()

    subject.attach(a)
    subject.attach(b)
    subject.change("first")

    subject.detach(b)
    subject.change("second")

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

// ---------- Observer interface ----------
interface Observer {
    void update(Subject subject);
}

// ---------- Subject ----------
class Subject {
    private final List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<>();

    public void attach(Observer observer) {
        observers.add(observer);
    }

    public void detach(Observer observer) {
        observers.remove(observer);
    }

    // NOT called notify() -- Object.notify() is final in Java
    public void notifyObservers() {
        for (Observer observer : new ArrayList<>(observers)) {
            observer.update(this);
        }
    }
}

// ---------- Concrete Subject ----------
class ConcreteSubject extends Subject {
    private String state;

    public void change(String value) {   // the state-changing operation ...
        this.state = value;
        notifyObservers();               // ... always ends with notifyObservers()
    }

    public String getState() {           // one reader per piece of state
        return state;
    }
}

// ---------- Concrete Observers ----------
class ConcreteObserverA implements Observer {
    @Override
    public void update(Subject subject) {
        String state = ((ConcreteSubject) subject).getState();   // pull, then print
        System.out.println("A saw " + state);
    }
}

class ConcreteObserverB implements Observer {
    @Override
    public void update(Subject subject) {
        String state = ((ConcreteSubject) subject).getState();
        System.out.println("B saw " + state);
    }
}

public class ObserverSkeleton {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ConcreteSubject subject = new ConcreteSubject();
        ConcreteObserverA a = new ConcreteObserverA();
        ConcreteObserverB b = new ConcreteObserverB();

        subject.attach(a);
        subject.attach(b);
        subject.change("first");

        subject.detach(b);
        subject.change("second");
    }
}
Output
A saw first
B saw first
A saw second

Rules that hold in every Observer solution

  • Subject.__init__ creates the list. The concrete subject calls super().__init__() — forgetting that line is the single most common bug in this pattern.
  • The state-changing method ends with self.notify(). Nothing else calls notify().
  • update takes the subject, not the data. The observer pulls what it needs through the getters, so adding a new field does not change the Observer interface.
  • One getter per piece of state, named the same in Python and Java.
  • The subject never knows a concrete observer type, and never imports one.

Singleton

Intent

Ensure a class has only one instance, and provide a global point of access to it.

One class plus its clients. The instance lives on the class, creation is guarded, and the clients never build one — they ask for it. The printed line inside the creation guard is there so you can see that it happens once; in a real singleton it would be the expensive thing you are trying not to repeat.

Python and Java disagree here more than anywhere else. Python overrides __new__; Java makes the constructor private and offers getInstance(). Same design, different mechanism.

RoleWhat it doesNotes
SingletonHolds _instance, guards creation, and does the real work.Everything one-per-program lives here.
ClientsAsk for the instance every time they need it. They never store it in a field, and never construct one.Any number of them.

# ---------- Singleton ----------
class Singleton:
    _instance = None                       # the one instance lives on the class

    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:          # lazy creation
            print("Creating the one instance...")
            cls._instance = super(Singleton, cls).__new__(cls)
            cls._instance.items = []       # initialise ONCE, here
        return cls._instance

    def record(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)
        total = len(self.items)
        print(f"recorded {item} (total {total})")

    def count(self):
        return len(self.items)


# ---------- Clients: each one asks for the instance independently ----------
class ClientA:
    def use(self, item):
        Singleton().record(item)


class ClientB:
    def report(self):
        count = Singleton().count()
        print(f"total so far: {count}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- nothing created yet ---")

    ClientA().use("first")
    ClientA().use("second")
    ClientB().report()

    same = Singleton() is Singleton()
    print("same object?", same)

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

// ---------- Singleton ----------
class Singleton {
    private static Singleton instance;                  // the one instance
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();

    private Singleton() {                               // nobody else can build one
        System.out.println("Creating the one instance...");
    }

    public static Singleton getInstance() {             // lazy creation
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new Singleton();
        }
        return instance;
    }

    public void record(String item) {
        items.add(item);
        int total = items.size();
        System.out.println("recorded " + item + " (total " + total + ")");
    }

    public int count() {
        return items.size();
    }
}

// ---------- Clients: each one asks for the instance independently ----------
class ClientA {
    public void use(String item) {
        Singleton.getInstance().record(item);
    }
}

class ClientB {
    public void report() {
        int count = Singleton.getInstance().count();
        System.out.println("total so far: " + count);
    }
}

public class SingletonSkeleton {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("--- nothing created yet ---");

        new ClientA().use("first");
        new ClientA().use("second");
        new ClientB().report();

        boolean same = Singleton.getInstance() == Singleton.getInstance();
        System.out.println("same object? " + same);
    }
}
Output — the two languages differ
--- nothing created yet ---
Creating the one instance...
recorded first (total 1)
recorded second (total 2)
total so far: 2
same object? True
--- nothing created yet ---
Creating the one instance...
recorded first (total 1)
recorded second (total 2)
total so far: 2
same object? true

Rules that hold in every Singleton solution

  • _instance is a class attribute, not an instance attribute.
  • The state is initialised inside the creation guard, so it happens once. Anything you initialise outside the guard is reset on every call.
  • In Python, __init__ still runs on every Singleton() call. If the class needs one, it must start with a guard — see Campus Alert Hub, where forgetting it silently empties the observer list.
  • Clients call Singleton() / Singleton.getInstance() at the point of use. A client that takes the instance as a constructor argument has removed the problem, not solved it.
  • The identity check a is b / a == b is the test that the pattern actually works.

Adapter

Intent

Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect.

Four roles. The adaptee is vendor code you are not allowed to touch — that constraint is the whole reason the pattern exists. The target is the interface your client wants to speak. The adapter implements the target and translates each call into whatever the adaptee actually offers. The client is written against the target and never learns a vendor name.

There are two ways to build the adapter. An object adapter holds the adaptee in a field; a class adapter inherits from it. Both appear below, and Checkout with Two Payment Vendors and Two Book Search Back-ends put them side by side. Everywhere else in this pack the object adapter is used, because it keeps the vendor methods off the adapter's public surface.

RoleWhat it doesNotes
AdapteeVendor code. Frozen — you may not edit it, and its method names are wrong for you.One or several.
TargetThe interface the client speaks. You design this one.An ABC in Python, an interface in Java.
AdapterImplements Target, translates each call into adaptee calls. One adapter per adaptee.Named <Vendor>Adapter.
ClientWritten against Target only.Never names a vendor class.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# ---------- Adaptee: vendor code, NOT modified ----------
class Vendor:
    def open_session(self):
        print("  Vendor: session opened")

    def vendor_call(self, a, b):
        print(f"  Vendor: working with {a} and {b}")
        return "vendor-result"


# ---------- Target ----------
class Target(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def request(self, value):
        pass


# ---------- Object Adapter (composition) ----------
class VendorObjectAdapter(Target):
    def __init__(self, adaptee):
        self.adaptee = adaptee                      # holds the adaptee

    def request(self, value):
        self.adaptee.open_session()                 # one target call ->
        return self.adaptee.vendor_call(value, 1)   # two adaptee calls


# ---------- Class Adapter (inheritance) ----------
class VendorClassAdapter(Target, Vendor):
    def request(self, value):
        self.open_session()                         # inherited, not held
        return self.vendor_call(value, 1)


# ---------- Client: speaks Target and nothing else ----------
class Client:
    def run(self, target):
        result = target.request("x")
        print("Client got:", result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    client = Client()

    client.run(VendorObjectAdapter(Vendor()))
    client.run(VendorClassAdapter())

// ---------- Adaptee: vendor code, NOT modified ----------
class Vendor {
    public void openSession() {
        System.out.println("  Vendor: session opened");
    }

    public String vendorCall(String a, int b) {
        System.out.println("  Vendor: working with " + a + " and " + b);
        return "vendor-result";
    }
}

// ---------- Target ----------
interface Target {
    String request(String value);
}

// ---------- Object Adapter (composition) ----------
class VendorObjectAdapter implements Target {
    private final Vendor adaptee;                       // holds the adaptee

    public VendorObjectAdapter(Vendor adaptee) {
        this.adaptee = adaptee;
    }

    @Override
    public String request(String value) {
        adaptee.openSession();                          // one target call ->
        return adaptee.vendorCall(value, 1);            // two adaptee calls
    }
}

// ---------- Class Adapter (inheritance) ----------
class VendorClassAdapter extends Vendor implements Target {
    @Override
    public String request(String value) {
        openSession();                                  // inherited, not held
        return vendorCall(value, 1);
    }
}

// ---------- Client: speaks Target and nothing else ----------
class Client {
    public void run(Target target) {
        String result = target.request("x");
        System.out.println("Client got: " + result);
    }
}

public class AdapterSkeleton {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Client client = new Client();

        client.run(new VendorObjectAdapter(new Vendor()));
        client.run(new VendorClassAdapter());
    }
}
Output
  Vendor: session opened
  Vendor: working with x and 1
Client got: vendor-result
  Vendor: session opened
  Vendor: working with x and 1
Client got: vendor-result

Rules that hold in every Adapter solution

  • The adaptee is never modified. If you edited it, you did not need the pattern.
  • One adapter per adaptee, named after the vendor it wraps and ending in Adapter.
  • The object adapter holds the vendor object in a field called adaptee and calls it. The class adapter inherits and calls the inherited method directly — that is the only difference.
  • Translation is the adapter's whole job: renaming, reordering, folding several vendor calls into one target call, converting units.
  • No vendor method name appears anywhere in the client. That is how you know the adapter is complete.

Factory Method

Intent

Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

Two parallel hierarchies. On the product side, an abstract Product holds whatever data every product needs and declares the abstract behaviour; each concrete product implements it. On the creator side, an abstract Creator declares the factory method — abstract, the one thing subclasses override — and a concrete template method that does the shared work using whatever the factory method returned.

The template method is the payoff. It is written once, names no concrete product, and contains no if on a type. Adding a fifth product means adding two classes and editing nothing.

RoleWhat it doesNotes
ProductAbstract. Constructor takes the data every product needs; declares the abstract behaviour.ABC in Python, abstract class in Java.
Concrete ProductsOne per variant. Implement the behaviour; add no new public methods.Usually three in these problems.
CreatorAbstract. Declares the abstract factory method and implements the concrete template method.The template method is the point.
Concrete CreatorsOverride the factory method, return one concrete product, and nothing else.One or two lines each.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# ---------- Product ----------
class Product(ABC):
    def __init__(self, data):           # every product is built with its data
        self.data = data

    @abstractmethod
    def describe(self):
        pass


# ---------- Concrete Products ----------
class ProductA(Product):
    def describe(self):
        return f"A({self.data})"


class ProductB(Product):
    def describe(self):
        return f"B({self.data})"


# ---------- Creator ----------
class Creator(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def create_product(self, data):     # the factory method
        pass

    def handle(self, data):             # the template method
        product = self.create_product(data)
        description = product.describe()
        print(f"handled {description}")


# ---------- Concrete Creators ----------
class CreatorA(Creator):
    def create_product(self, data):
        return ProductA(data)


class CreatorB(Creator):
    def create_product(self, data):
        return ProductB(data)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    creators = [CreatorA(), CreatorB()]

    for creator in creators:
        creator.handle("input")

// ---------- Product ----------
abstract class Product {
    protected final String data;        // every product is built with its data

    protected Product(String data) {
        this.data = data;
    }

    public abstract String describe();
}

// ---------- Concrete Products ----------
class ProductA extends Product {
    public ProductA(String data) {
        super(data);
    }

    @Override
    public String describe() {
        return "A(" + data + ")";
    }
}

class ProductB extends Product {
    public ProductB(String data) {
        super(data);
    }

    @Override
    public String describe() {
        return "B(" + data + ")";
    }
}

// ---------- Creator ----------
abstract class Creator {
    protected abstract Product createProduct(String data);   // the factory method

    public void handle(String data) {                        // the template method
        Product product = createProduct(data);
        String description = product.describe();
        System.out.println("handled " + description);
    }
}

// ---------- Concrete Creators ----------
class CreatorA extends Creator {
    @Override
    protected Product createProduct(String data) {
        return new ProductA(data);
    }
}

class CreatorB extends Creator {
    @Override
    protected Product createProduct(String data) {
        return new ProductB(data);
    }
}

public class FactoryMethodSkeleton {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Creator[] creators = {new CreatorA(), new CreatorB()};

        for (Creator creator : creators) {
            creator.handle("input");
        }
    }
}
Output
handled A(input)
handled B(input)

Rules that hold in every Factory Method solution

  • The factory method is abstract on the creator and overridden in every concrete creator.
  • The template method is concrete on the creator and is never overridden.
  • The template method names no concrete product and contains no if/elif on a type string. If one survives, the pattern was not applied.
  • The factory method takes whatever data the product needs to be built, and the template method forwards it. Sometimes that is nothing.
  • A concrete creator returns something already conforming to Product. Returning a raw object for the template method to fix up puts the decision straight back where it came from.

The Section Notice Board

Push, don't poll

The story

The CSE470 section page has one notice board. Whenever the instructor posts something new, every student currently enrolled in that section must find out immediately — nobody should have to keep refreshing the page to check whether something changed. Students join and leave the section throughout the drop-add week, and the section has no idea how many will be listening on any given day.

The department also wants a notice archive that quietly records every posted notice — it is not a student, but it wants the same updates.

The section must not keep any student-specific logic inside it. All it knows is that whatever is listening can be told “something changed.”

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# ---------- Observer interface ----------
class Observer(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def update(self, subject):
        pass


# ---------- Subject ----------
class Subject:
    def __init__(self):
        self._observers = []

    def attach(self, observer):
        self._observers.append(observer)

    def detach(self, observer):
        if observer in self._observers:
            self._observers.remove(observer)

    def notify(self):
        for observer in self._observers:
            observer.update(self)


# ---------- Concrete Subject ----------
class CourseSection(Subject):
    def __init__(self, code):
        super().__init__()
        self._code = code
        self._latest_notice = None

    def post_notice(self, text):
        self._latest_notice = text
        self.notify()

    def get_code(self):
        return self._code

    def get_notice(self):
        return self._latest_notice


# ---------- Concrete Observers ----------
class Student(Observer):
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def update(self, subject):
        code = subject.get_code()
        notice = subject.get_notice()
        print(f"[{self.name}] {code} -> {notice}")

    def enroll(self, section):
        section.attach(self)
        code = section.get_code()
        print(f"{self.name} enrolled in {code}")

    def drop(self, section):
        section.detach(self)
        code = section.get_code()
        print(f"{self.name} dropped {code}")


class NoticeArchive(Observer):
    def __init__(self):
        self.log = []

    def update(self, subject):
        code = subject.get_code()
        notice = subject.get_notice()
        self.log.append(f"{code} :: {notice}")
        count = len(self.log)
        print(f"[Archive] saved notice #{count}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cse470 = CourseSection("CSE470-01")

    rafi = Student("Rafi")
    tanha = Student("Tanha")
    archive = NoticeArchive()

    rafi.enroll(cse470)
    tanha.enroll(cse470)
    cse470.attach(archive)

    cse470.post_notice("Quiz 2 on Sunday")

    tanha.drop(cse470)
    cse470.post_notice("Project proposal deadline extended")

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

// ---------- Observer interface ----------
interface Observer {
    void update(Subject subject);
}

// ---------- Subject ----------
class Subject {
    private final List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<>();

    public void attach(Observer observer) {
        observers.add(observer);
    }

    public void detach(Observer observer) {
        observers.remove(observer);
    }

    // NOT called notify() -- Object.notify() is final in Java
    public void notifyObservers() {
        for (Observer observer : new ArrayList<>(observers)) {
            observer.update(this);
        }
    }
}

// ---------- Concrete Subject ----------
class CourseSection extends Subject {
    private final String code;
    private String latestNotice;

    public CourseSection(String code) {
        this.code = code;
    }

    public void postNotice(String text) {
        this.latestNotice = text;
        notifyObservers();
    }

    public String getCode() {
        return code;
    }

    public String getNotice() {
        return latestNotice;
    }
}

// ---------- Concrete Observers ----------
class Student implements Observer {
    private final String name;

    public Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public void update(Subject subject) {
        CourseSection section = (CourseSection) subject;
        String code = section.getCode();
        String notice = section.getNotice();
        System.out.println("[" + name + "] " + code + " -> " + notice);
    }

    public void enroll(CourseSection section) {
        section.attach(this);
        String code = section.getCode();
        System.out.println(name + " enrolled in " + code);
    }

    public void drop(CourseSection section) {
        section.detach(this);
        String code = section.getCode();
        System.out.println(name + " dropped " + code);
    }
}

class NoticeArchive implements Observer {
    private final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public void update(Subject subject) {
        CourseSection section = (CourseSection) subject;
        String code = section.getCode();
        String notice = section.getNotice();
        log.add(code + " :: " + notice);
        int count = log.size();
        System.out.println("[Archive] saved notice #" + count);
    }
}

public class NoticeBoardDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CourseSection cse470 = new CourseSection("CSE470-01");

        Student rafi = new Student("Rafi");
        Student tanha = new Student("Tanha");
        NoticeArchive archive = new NoticeArchive();

        rafi.enroll(cse470);
        tanha.enroll(cse470);
        cse470.attach(archive);

        cse470.postNotice("Quiz 2 on Sunday");

        tanha.drop(cse470);
        cse470.postNotice("Project proposal deadline extended");
    }
}
Output
Rafi enrolled in CSE470-01
Tanha enrolled in CSE470-01
[Rafi] CSE470-01 -> Quiz 2 on Sunday
[Tanha] CSE470-01 -> Quiz 2 on Sunday
[Archive] saved notice #1
Tanha dropped CSE470-01
[Rafi] CSE470-01 -> Project proposal deadline extended
[Archive] saved notice #2

Participants

RoleClass
ObserverObserver
SubjectSubject
Concrete SubjectCourseSection
Concrete ObserversStudent, NoticeArchive

Marking points

  • notify() is called from inside post_notice, not from the driver — the update must be pushed.
  • CourseSection never names Student anywhere. If it does, the one-to-many decoupling is not there.
  • detach actually removes, and the dropped student produces no output on the second notice.
  • NoticeArchive proves observers need not be homogeneous. A solution that only has students still passes, but loses this point.

Java notes — where the translation is not one-to-one

  • notify() is final on java.lang.Object, so the subject's broadcast method has to be named something else — notifyObservers() is the conventional choice.
  • update(Subject) forces a downcast in each observer. The alternative is a generic interface Observer<S> { void update(S subject); }, which removes the cast at the price of generics noise — worth showing once.
  • Iterating over a copy of the list (new ArrayList<>(observers)) avoids ConcurrentModificationException if an observer detaches itself during update. Python's for loop over a list has the same hazard, silently.
Practice — Set ASingleton

One Grade Database

Exactly one, created late

The story

The result processing system has several independent modules: the quiz module, the transcript module, the scholarship module. Each one currently opens its own connection to the grade database. That means a grade saved by the quiz module is invisible to the transcript module, and the server logs show one expensive connection per module.

The university wants exactly one grade database object for the whole system, reachable from anywhere, and it must not be created at program start-up — the connection should only open the first time some module actually needs it.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

class GradeDatabase {
    Map<String, Double> records;

    GradeDatabase() {
        System.out.println("Opening connection to grade database...");
        this.records = new HashMap<>();
    }

    void save(String studentId, double grade) {
        records.put(studentId, grade);
        System.out.println("saved " + studentId + " = " + grade);
    }

    String get(String studentId) {
        Double grade = records.get(studentId);
        return grade == null ? "not found" : String.valueOf(grade);
    }
}

class QuizModule {
    void submit(String studentId, double grade) {
        GradeDatabase db = new GradeDatabase();
        db.save(studentId, grade);
    }
}

class TranscriptModule {
    void show(String studentId) {
        GradeDatabase db = new GradeDatabase();
        System.out.println("transcript of " + studentId + ": " + db.get(studentId));
    }
}

Your task

  • Transform GradeDatabase so every GradeDatabase() call hands back the same object.
  • Do not change QuizModule or TranscriptModule at all — they must keep calling GradeDatabase() normally.
  • Careful: __init__ runs on every call. Make sure re-entering it does not wipe the records you already saved.
  • Driver: let the quiz module save a grade, then let the transcript module read it back, then print an identity check on two fresh handles.

# ---------- Singleton ----------
class GradeDatabase:
    _instance = None

    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._instance is None:                 # lazy creation
            print("Opening connection to grade database...")
            cls._instance = super(GradeDatabase, cls).__new__(cls)
            cls._instance.records = {}            # initialise ONCE, here
        return cls._instance

    def save(self, student_id, grade):
        self.records[student_id] = grade
        print(f"saved {student_id} = {grade}")

    def get(self, student_id):
        return self.records.get(student_id, "not found")


# ---------- Clients: each one asks for the database independently ----------
class QuizModule:
    def submit(self, student_id, grade):
        db = GradeDatabase()
        db.save(student_id, grade)


class TranscriptModule:
    def show(self, student_id):
        db = GradeDatabase()
        grade = db.get(student_id)
        print(f"transcript of {student_id}: {grade}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- system starting, no database touched yet ---")

    quiz = QuizModule()
    transcript = TranscriptModule()

    quiz.submit("21301001", 3.75)

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

// ---------- Singleton ----------
class GradeDatabase {
    private static GradeDatabase instance;                    // the one instance
    private final Map<String, Double> records = new HashMap<>();

    private GradeDatabase() {                                 // nobody else can build one
        System.out.println("Opening connection to grade database...");
    }

    public static GradeDatabase getInstance() {               // lazy creation
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new GradeDatabase();
        }
        return instance;
    }

    public void save(String studentId, double grade) {
        records.put(studentId, grade);
        System.out.println("saved " + studentId + " = " + grade);
    }

    public String get(String studentId) {
        Double grade = records.get(studentId);
        return grade == null ? "not found" : String.valueOf(grade);
    }
}

// ---------- Clients: each one asks for the database independently ----------
class QuizModule {
    void submit(String studentId, double grade) {
        GradeDatabase.getInstance().save(studentId, grade);
    }
}

class TranscriptModule {
    void show(String studentId) {
        GradeDatabase db = GradeDatabase.getInstance();
        String grade = db.get(studentId);
        System.out.println("transcript of " + studentId + ": " + grade);
    }
}

public class GradeDatabaseDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("--- system starting, no database touched yet ---");

        QuizModule quiz = new QuizModule();
        TranscriptModule transcript = new TranscriptModule();

        quiz.submit("21301001", 3.75);
        transcript.show("21301001");

        GradeDatabase a = GradeDatabase.getInstance();
        GradeDatabase b = GradeDatabase.getInstance();
        System.out.println("same object? " + (a == b));
    }
}
Output — the two languages differ
--- system starting, no database touched yet ---
Opening connection to grade database...

transcript of 21301001: 3.75
same object? True
--- system starting, no database touched yet ---
Opening connection to grade database...
saved 21301001 = 3.75
transcript of 21301001: 3.75
same object? true

Marking points

  • __new__ is overridden, _instance is a class attribute, and the guard is if cls._instance is None — this is what makes it lazy.
  • The connection message prints once and only after the first client asks. A solution that creates the instance at import time is not lazy.
  • records is initialised inside the __new__ guard (or with an _initialised flag in __init__). A plain __init__ that assigns self.records = {} wipes the data on every later call — the transcript then prints not found. This is the trap in this problem.
  • Identity check prints True.
  • Common alternatives worth accepting: a get_instance() classmethod, a decorator, or a module-level instance — but ask them to justify laziness in each case.

Java notes — where the translation is not one-to-one

  • Java has no __new__. A constructor always produces a fresh object, so the Python trick of “return the existing instance from the constructor” simply cannot be written. The only form is a private constructor plus a static getInstance().
  • That means the clients must change: new GradeDatabase() becomes GradeDatabase.getInstance(). The Python brief's “don't touch the clients” rule is a Python-specific luxury — point this out, it is the sharpest language difference in the set.
  • Python prints True; Java prints true. The Output panel above has its own Python/Java tabs wherever the two runs genuinely differ — this is the only reason any of them do.
  • The Python trap (__init__ re-running and wiping state) disappears in Java, because the constructor only runs when an object is genuinely created. Java's equivalent trap is thread safety: two threads can both see instance == null. Production forms are the holder idiom (private static class Holder { static final GradeDatabase INSTANCE = ...; }), a synchronized accessor, or simply enum Singleton { INSTANCE; }.

Checkout with Two Payment Vendors

Object adapter vs class adapter

The story

Your online store's checkout screen wants to treat every payment method the same way: charge an amount in taka, then produce a receipt.

Two payment providers are already integrated, and you cannot edit either of them — they ship as a vendor SDK and any change is lost on the next update. Unfortunately their interfaces do not match yours: the bKash class names its methods differently, and the old card terminal both names things differently and expects the amount in poisha, not taka.

Read it first

The Java snippet does not compile as it stands — Checkout names a Payment type that does not exist yet. That is not a mistake: it is task 1, and the compiler is telling you the interface is missing. Python lets the same file load happily and only fails when process is actually called.

Your task

  • Wrap BkashGateway using an object adapter (composition).
  • Wrap LegacyCardTerminal using a class adapter (inheritance). The taka → poisha conversion is the adapter's job, not the client's.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# ---------- Adaptees: vendor code, NOT modified ----------
class BkashGateway:
    def execute_payment(self, taka):
        print(f"bKash: BDT {taka} debited from wallet")

    def send_sms_receipt(self):
        print("bKash: SMS receipt sent")


class LegacyCardTerminal:
    def swipe_card(self):
        print("Terminal: card swiped")

    def charge_amount(self, poisha):
        print(f"Terminal: charged {poisha} poisha")

    def print_slip(self):
        print("Terminal: paper slip printed")


# ---------- Target ----------
class Payment(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def pay(self, taka):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def receipt(self):
        pass


# ---------- Object Adapter (composition) ----------
class BkashObjectAdapter(Payment):
    def __init__(self, adaptee):
        self.adaptee = adaptee

    def pay(self, taka):
        self.adaptee.execute_payment(taka)

    def receipt(self):
        self.adaptee.send_sms_receipt()


# ---------- Class Adapter (inheritance) ----------
class CardClassAdapter(Payment, LegacyCardTerminal):
    def pay(self, taka):
        self.swipe_card()
        self.charge_amount(int(taka * 100))     # unit conversion lives here

    def receipt(self):
        self.print_slip()


# ---------- Client ----------
class Checkout:
    def process(self, payment, taka):
        print(f"Checkout: collecting BDT {taka}")
        payment.pay(taka)
        payment.receipt()
        print("Checkout: done\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    checkout = Checkout()

    bkash = BkashObjectAdapter(BkashGateway())
    card = CardClassAdapter()

    for method in (bkash, card):
        checkout.process(method, 250.50)

// ---------- Adaptees: vendor code, NOT modified ----------
class BkashGateway {
    void executePayment(double taka) {
        System.out.println("bKash: BDT " + taka + " debited from wallet");
    }

    void sendSmsReceipt() {
        System.out.println("bKash: SMS receipt sent");
    }
}

class LegacyCardTerminal {
    void swipeCard() {
        System.out.println("Terminal: card swiped");
    }

    void chargeAmount(long poisha) {
        System.out.println("Terminal: charged " + poisha + " poisha");
    }

    void printSlip() {
        System.out.println("Terminal: paper slip printed");
    }
}

// ---------- Target ----------
interface Payment {
    void pay(double taka);

    void receipt();
}

// ---------- Object Adapter (composition) ----------
class BkashObjectAdapter implements Payment {
    private final BkashGateway adaptee;

    public BkashObjectAdapter(BkashGateway adaptee) {
        this.adaptee = adaptee;
    }

    @Override
    public void pay(double taka) {
        adaptee.executePayment(taka);
    }

    @Override
    public void receipt() {
        adaptee.sendSmsReceipt();
    }
}

// ---------- Class Adapter (inheritance) ----------
class CardClassAdapter extends LegacyCardTerminal implements Payment {
    @Override
    public void pay(double taka) {
        swipeCard();
        chargeAmount(Math.round(taka * 100));       // unit conversion lives here
    }

    @Override
    public void receipt() {
        printSlip();
    }
}

// ---------- Client ----------
class Checkout {
    void process(Payment payment, double taka) {
        System.out.println("Checkout: collecting BDT " + taka);
        payment.pay(taka);
        payment.receipt();
        System.out.println("Checkout: done\n");
    }
}

public class CheckoutDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Checkout checkout = new Checkout();

        Payment bkash = new BkashObjectAdapter(new BkashGateway());
        Payment card = new CardClassAdapter();

        for (Payment method : new Payment[]{bkash, card}) {
            checkout.process(method, 250.50);
        }
    }
}

Marking points

  • Neither vendor class is edited. Any change there is an automatic deduction.
  • Object adapter holds the adaptee as an attribute; class adapter inherits from Payment and the adaptee.
  • The * 100 conversion sits in the adapter, never in Checkout.
  • Checkout.process is unchanged and is called identically for both methods.

Java notes — where the translation is not one-to-one

  • Java has no multiple inheritance of classes, so the class adapter is written extends LegacyCardTerminal implements Payment — one class, any number of interfaces. It only works here because the target is an interface. In Python, class CardClassAdapter(Payment, LegacyCardTerminal) inherits from two real classes.
  • That is exactly why the GoF book presents the class adapter as a C++ idiom and the object adapter as the portable one: in a single-inheritance language the class adapter spends your one inheritance slot.
  • int(taka * 100) truncates in Python, and a Java cast does the same — which is why the solution uses Math.round. This amount is safe either way (250.5 is exactly representable, so both give 25050), but the habit is not: (long)(1.15 * 100) is 114, while Math.round(1.15 * 100) is 115. Worth demonstrating live — it is the shortest convincing argument for BigDecimal, or for holding money as integer poisha end to end.

Follow-up answers

1.Which of the two adapters could also have wrapped an object you receive at runtime, and why can the other one not?

The object adapter can wrap an instance handed to it at runtime (composition — you can even swap the adaptee later, or wrap a subclass). The class adapter fixes its adaptee at class-definition time through inheritance, so it can only ever adapt that one class.

Practice — Set AFactory Method

The Courier Branch

Let the subclass decide what to build

The story

A courier company books three kinds of shipment: standard, express and international. Each kind prints a different label and calculates fare differently.

Every branch office follows the exact same booking routine: create the shipment, print its label, then quote the fare. The routine never changes. What changes is which kind of shipment a particular branch produces — the airport branch only books international, the city branch only books standard, and so on.

Right now the booking routine is stuck with an if/elif chain, so opening a new branch type means editing the routine that every branch shares. The branch knows when a shipment must be created; it should not be the place that decides what kind.

class StandardShipment:
    def label(self):
        print("Label: STANDARD - delivery in 5 days")

    def cost(self, kg):
        return 60 * kg


class ExpressShipment:
    def label(self):
        print("Label: EXPRESS - delivery in 24 hours")

    def cost(self, kg):
        return 150 * kg


class InternationalShipment:
    def label(self):
        print("Label: INTERNATIONAL - customs form attached")

    def cost(self, kg):
        return 900 * kg + 500


class DeliveryOffice:
    def handle_order(self, kind, kg):
        if kind == "standard":
            shipment = StandardShipment()
        elif kind == "express":
            shipment = ExpressShipment()
        else:
            shipment = InternationalShipment()
        shipment.label()
        print(f"Booked {kg} kg, fare BDT {shipment.cost(kg)}\n")

        if (kind.equals("standard")) {
            StandardShipment shipment = new StandardShipment();

        } else {
            InternationalShipment shipment = new InternationalShipment();
            shipment.label();
            System.out.println("Booked " + kg + " kg, fare BDT " + shipment.cost(kg) + "\n");

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# ---------- Product ----------
class Shipment(ABC):
    def __init__(self, weight_kg):      # every product is built with its data
        self.weight_kg = weight_kg

    @abstractmethod
    def label(self):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def cost(self):
        pass


# ---------- Concrete Products ----------
class StandardShipment(Shipment):
    def label(self):
        print("Label: STANDARD - delivery in 5 days")

    def cost(self):
        return 60 * self.weight_kg


class ExpressShipment(Shipment):
    def label(self):
        print("Label: EXPRESS - delivery in 24 hours")

    def cost(self):
        return 150 * self.weight_kg


class InternationalShipment(Shipment):
    def label(self):
        print("Label: INTERNATIONAL - customs form attached")

    def cost(self):
        return 900 * self.weight_kg + 500


# ---------- Creator ----------
class DeliveryOffice(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def create_shipment(self, kg):      # the factory method
        pass

    def handle_order(self, kg):         # the template method
        shipment = self.create_shipment(kg)
        shipment.label()
        fare = shipment.cost()
        print(f"Booked {kg} kg, fare BDT {fare}\n")


# ---------- Concrete Creators ----------
class StandardOffice(DeliveryOffice):
    def create_shipment(self, kg):
        return StandardShipment(kg)


class ExpressOffice(DeliveryOffice):
    def create_shipment(self, kg):
        return ExpressShipment(kg)


class InternationalOffice(DeliveryOffice):
    def create_shipment(self, kg):
        return InternationalShipment(kg)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    offices = [StandardOffice(), ExpressOffice(), InternationalOffice()]

    for office in offices:
        office.handle_order(2)

    public void handleOrder(int kg) {                    // the template method

class ExpressOffice extends DeliveryOffice {

Marking points

  • create_shipment is abstract on DeliveryOffice and overridden in each subclass.
  • handle_order keeps the invariant routine and calls self.create_shipment(kg) — it never names a concrete shipment class.
  • No if/elif on a type string anywhere, and handle_order no longer takes a kind argument.
  • Driver treats all three offices through the base type.

Java notes — where the translation is not one-to-one

  • Look at the given Java code above: because the three shipment classes share no supertype, Java will not even let you write shipment = ... once outside the chain. The whole routine has to be duplicated three times. Python's duck typing hides that cost; Java makes the missing abstraction impossible to ignore.
  • The factory method is protected abstract, not public. It exists for the subclass to answer, not for clients to call — Python has no way to say that.
  • Java's covariant return types let StandardOffice.createShipment(kg) be declared as returning StandardShipment instead of Shipment if a subclass genuinely needs the narrower type.

Follow-up answers

1.To add a “drone delivery” branch, which existing files or classes must you edit? Compare with the given code.

Only two additions — a DroneShipment product and a DroneOffice creator. Nothing existing is edited. In the given code, handle_order itself had to be reopened, which is exactly the closed-for-modification violation the pattern removes.

Practice — Set BObserver

The Online Auction Room

Push, don't poll

The story

An online auction runs one item at a time. The moment a higher bid arrives, every bidder sitting in the room must see the new price at once — nobody should have to keep clicking refresh to find out they have been outbid. Bidders walk in and walk out while the auction is running, and the auction has no idea how many will be watching at any moment.

The auction house also runs a bid logger that records every price change for dispute resolution. It is not a bidder, but it wants exactly the same updates.

The auction object must not contain any bidder-specific logic. All it knows is that whatever is watching can be told “the price changed.”

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


# ---------- Observer interface ----------
class Observer(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def update(self, subject):
        pass


# ---------- Subject ----------
class Subject:
    def __init__(self):
        self._observers = []

    def attach(self, observer):
        self._observers.append(observer)

    def detach(self, observer):
        if observer in self._observers:
            self._observers.remove(observer)

    def notify(self):
        for observer in self._observers:
            observer.update(self)


# ---------- Concrete Subject ----------
class Auction(Subject):
    def __init__(self, item):
        super().__init__()
        self._item = item
        self._highest_bid = 0
        self._highest_bidder = "nobody"

    def place_bid(self, name, amount):
        if amount > self._highest_bid:
            self._highest_bid = amount
            self._highest_bidder = name
            self.notify()

    def get_item(self):
        return self._item

    def get_highest_bid(self):
        return self._highest_bid

    def get_highest_bidder(self):
        return self._highest_bidder


# ---------- Concrete Observers ----------
class Bidder(Observer):
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def update(self, subject):
        item = subject.get_item()
        amount = subject.get_highest_bid()
        leader = subject.get_highest_bidder()
        tag = "you lead" if leader == self.name else f"{leader} leads"
        print(f"[{self.name}] {item} now BDT {amount} - {tag}")

    def join(self, auction):
        auction.attach(self)
        print(f"{self.name} joined the auction")

    def leave(self, auction):
        auction.detach(self)
        print(f"{self.name} left the auction")


class BidLogger(Observer):
    def __init__(self):
        self.entries = []

    def update(self, subject):
        amount = subject.get_highest_bid()
        leader = subject.get_highest_bidder()
        self.entries.append((amount, leader))
        count = len(self.entries)
        print(f"[Logger] bid #{count} recorded")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    auction = Auction("Antique Clock")

    nabil = Bidder("Nabil")
    sadia = Bidder("Sadia")
    logger = BidLogger()

    nabil.join(auction)
    sadia.join(auction)
    auction.attach(logger)

    auction.place_bid("Nabil", 5000)
    sadia.leave(auction)
    auction.place_bid("Sadia", 7500)
